solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Sounds like Dick O'Front's a dish

indicators.note: sounds like says the answer is heard as the words built from the clue

parts.note: dick is slang for cock, O' is kept, and front is van (as in vanguard), giving cock o' van

explanation.surface: A rude-sounding name, Dick O'Front, is claimed to be a dish, in Private Eye style.
explanation.definitionFit: Coq au vin is a French recipe of chicken braised in red wine.

clue.text: Sadly no lady (the sort Thatcher was) — rather old-fashioned air

indicators.note: something done sadly is done badly, so the letters come out in a poor, jumbled order

parts.note: letters to be rearranged
Margaret Thatcher was nicknamed the Iron Lady

explanation.surface: A dig at Thatcher, followed by a remark that something has a dated feel to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis completes 'lady' in the surface, but cryptically it supplies the kind of lady Thatcher was.
explanation.definitionFit: Any Old Iron is a cockney music-hall song from 1911, so an old-fashioned air, air meaning tune.

clue.text: Private Eye takes on City, Brenda and Santander's main shady lenders

parts.note: the magazine speaking of itself: we, us
Ur, the ancient Sumerian city, a crossword favourite
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth, whose cipher is ER

indicators.note: the main or leading part of the word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the first letter of the bank's name

explanation.surface: The magazine takes on the City, the Queen and a big bank as a pack of shady moneylenders.
explanation.walkthrough: Santander is a Spanish-owned bank on British high streets; Brenda is the Eye's long-running name for the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Usurers lend money at exorbitant interest, which makes them disreputable lenders.

clue.text: (& 12ac.) Feeling bad following party? Shun government's division

indicators.note: a division is a section cut out of something larger, so the answer is a slice of the clue's letters

parts.note: the run of letters after the opening S of the first word and through the start of the second

explanation.surface: A political question about shunning the government after a party, with a hint at a hung parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'party' and 'government' suggest politics, and 'hung' parliament lurks in the reading too.
explanation.definitionFit: Being hung over is the sick, headachy state after drinking too much at a party the night before.

clue.text: Gordon really starts to chomp — idiot gets the bird

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, so only the openings of the two words are kept

parts.note: first letters of the two words
to chomp is to eat
British slang for a fool

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown is ridiculed for his eating habits and is given the bird by the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting the bird means being jeered, which suits the surface; cryptically 'the bird' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The great tit is a common European songbird with a black head and yellow front.

clue.text: Fancy Jack Straw's introductions, do we? No! (A low indicator of present depressed times)

definitions.text: A low indicator of present depressed times

indicators.note: fancy as a verb invites us to imagine the letters made into something fanciful, a fresh order
an introduction comes first, so each of the two names gives only its opening letter

parts.note: first letters of the two names
letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A sneer at Jack Straw, the Labour minister, with a gloomy aside on the economy.
explanation.walkthrough: Written during the 2008-09 crash, when the stock indices were at record lows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dow Jones is the leading US share index, an economic gauge that sank in the recession.

clue.text: Judgemental type Jack "upset our party's centre"

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in playing cards

indicators.note: when something is upset its parts are knocked out of order

parts.note: letters rearranged

indicators.note: the centre of a five-letter word is its single middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of the five

explanation.surface: Jack Straw passes judgement, accused of having upset the core of the Labour party.
explanation.definitionFit: A juror sits on a jury and delivers a verdict, so is literally someone who judges.

clue.text: Sun restrained?! It shows the turmoil

indicators.note: the clue's own words display the answer, which is on show inside them

parts.note: the run from the second letter of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A jibe at the Sun newspaper for showing restraint, the shock of it causing chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid famous for anything but restraint, hence the ?!.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrest is a state of disturbance and agitation, a near synonym of turmoil.

clue.text: Streak, everything off, small organ

indicators.note: off means taken away, so a whole word is removed from the next one

parts.note: taken as written
everything is all
the organ of hearing

explanation.surface: A streaker strips off completely and reveals a small organ.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Streak, everything off' paints a naked dash; really 'everything' is cut from the word next to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A smear is a streak or mark of something spread across a surface.

clue.text: Hillary's first broadcast act, shock style

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter alone of the name before it

parts.note: first letter of the name
to broadcast a programme is to air it
to act is to do

explanation.surface: Hillary Clinton's first televised appearance produces a shock in style terms.
explanation.walkthrough: A shock here is a mass of hair, not a fright; the style of it is how it is cut and set.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairdo is the style in which a head of hair, a shock, is arranged.

clue.text: Mark again has, er, bent over Michael

indicators.note: bent means twisted out of shape, so the letters of er are rearranged

parts.note: Michael Grade is a British TV executive and former BBC chairman

explanation.surface: A man hesitating, er, bends over someone called Michael.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Grade ran Channel 4 and chaired the BBC, a regular target in Private Eye.
explanation.definitionFit: To regrade is to assess or score work once more, giving it a new mark.

clue.text: see 4dn.
Back-stabbed e.g. David Cameron, being disrespectful

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word that follows from its end to its start

parts.note: stabbed with horns, as by a bull
Cameron was a Tory, a member of the Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Cameron, betrayed by colleagues, in a scornful political aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Back-stabbed looks like a single compound word; split, 'Back' is the signal and 'stabbed' is the word it acts on.
explanation.definitionFit: Derogatory remarks belittle someone, showing a lack of respect.

clue.text: Glam celebs refuse one when collared by stupid git

indicators.note: being collared is being grabbed round the neck, so the rearranged git letters surround the others
stupid suggests muddled, so the letters of git are rearranged

parts.note: litter is refuse or rubbish
A means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: Showbiz stars turn down someone grabbed by a foolish idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refuse' looks like a verb meaning decline, but it is the noun, rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: The glitterati are fashionable, glamorous celebrities, a blend of glitter and literati.

clue.text: (& 17/23) Fickle public's changed opinion of Obama? Expect mean behaviour from now on

definitions.text: Fickle public's changed opinion of Obama?
definitions.meaning: first meaning: once seen as a decent chap, the president is no longer viewed that way

definitions.text: Expect mean behaviour from now on
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a stock phrase announcing that the gloves are coming off

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: a voter turning on Obama would say he is no longer the decent fellow they thought. The question mark flags that playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying is a warning that someone is done being pleasant and will now act tough.

clue.text: Guy with laces undone as a bondage aid?

definitions.note: a set of manacles is one item, so the singular definition fits the plural word

parts.note: a guy is a man

indicators.note: laces that are undone come loose, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man whose laces have come undone serves as a bondage aid.
explanation.definitionFit: Manacles are shackles for the hands, used for restraint.

clue.text: see 15ac.
Callous as Brown's cabinet was when Kelly went

definitions.text: Brown's cabinet was when Kelly went
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Ruth Kelly quit Gordon Brown's cabinet in 2008, leaving it lacking her

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a pun: without Ruth Kelly the cabinet was Ruth-less. Kelly was Brown's Transport Secretary until she resigned.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruthless means having no pity or compassion, which is what callous means.

clue.text: Cameron's brand of politics will bring you to dire, energy-drained misery!

indicators.note: dire suggests something in a terrible state, so the letters are thrown into disorder
E for energy is drained out of the word misery, leaving its other letters

parts.note: the word misery, which loses its E before being rearranged

explanation.surface: A satirical jibe that David Cameron's politics will lead voters to grim, exhausted misery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dire' looks like part of the gloomy picture, but it is the signal to rearrange what is left once the energy letter has gone.
explanation.definitionFit: David Cameron led the Conservative Party, whose members are called Tories, so his political creed is Toryism.

clue.text: "Bum hair as well," declared gay

parts.note: down is fine, soft hair
and means also
someone who has come out has openly declared being gay

explanation.surface: A camp quote about bottoms and body hair, announced by a gay man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as backside; it is the American sense, a tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: A bum is a vagrant, someone destitute and homeless, exactly a down-and-out.

clue.text: British forsaking Brown — about over, he admits

indicators.note: British abandons the surname, so those letters are removed from its front

parts.note: taken as the name, as in Gordon Brown

indicators.note: over signals that the word for about is turned round

parts.note: RE is Latin-derived for about or concerning

explanation.surface: A political report: the British desert Gordon Brown, and someone owns up to it.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking BR from BROWN leaves OWN; RE turned over gives ER. 'He admits' is cryptic: one who owns up, an owner.
explanation.definitionFit: To own something is also to admit it, so playfully a person who owns up is an owner.

clue.text: Things agreed: removing tip of penis has an effect

indicators.note: removing means taking something away, so that letter goes

parts.note: pacts are agreements

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its very first letter

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Circumcision is agreed to, and is said to have an effect.
explanation.definitionFit: A medicine that acts works, producing an effect on the body.

clue.text: Cruising Med in one? They'll supply plugs

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters within the word for one

parts.note: an means one, as in a single thing

indicators.note: cruising means moving about, so the letters of Med are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone cruising the Mediterranean on a boat that has power sockets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plugs' suggests electrical sockets, but here a plug is a piece of advertising.
explanation.definitionFit: Admen work in advertising, and a plug is a promotional mention of a product.

clue.text: see 15ac.
Personal ad requirement: "heart transplant needed" — bloody hell!

indicators.note: the middle part of the abbreviation is moved around, as in an operation on the heart

parts.note: lonely-hearts shorthand for good sense of humour

explanation.surface: A lonely-hearts ad stipulating a heart transplant, which draws a shocked exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: GSOH, good sense of humour, is the standard abbreviation in British dating ads; only its two central letters swap.
explanation.definitionFit: Gosh and bloody hell are both exclamations of surprise, one mild and one strong.

clue.text: Boom means heads of merchant banks breaking injunction

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it

parts.note: an injunction is an order, a rule

indicators.note: the heads of words are their first letters

parts.note: first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A boom period means banking bosses flouting court orders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boom' suggests economic good times; it is the noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumble is a deep, resonant sound like a boom of thunder.

clue.text: Shorts accepted by defenders

definitions.meaning: second meaning: instructions that a defence barrister takes on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests footballers in shorts; the defenders are courtroom lawyers.
explanation.definitionFit: Briefs are both short underpants and the case instructions given to barristers acting for a client.

clue.text: Follower of Nick Brown's inside as it's gone pear-shaped

indicators.note: Brown's inside means the brown word sits within the rearranged letters
gone pear-shaped means gone wrong, so the letters of as it's are rearranged

parts.note: tan is a shade of brown

explanation.surface: Nick Brown, a politician, is in office as everything collapses.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Brown is a Labour MP, but here Old Nick is the Devil; 'gone pear-shaped' is British slang for gone wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A Satanist worships Satan, who is called Old Nick in English folk usage.
